questions.q: What is the typical basic structure of quant compensation across most firm types?
options: A fixed hourly wage with no variable component
A base salary plus an annual bonus, with the bonus as the variable component
Payment entirely in company equity with no cash component
A single lump-sum payment made once at hiring
questions.explain: Total compensation is typically structured as a relatively stable base salary plus a variable annual bonus, which is where most of the difference between a strong year and a weak year shows up.

questions.q: What is commonly used as the basis for an individual's annual bonus?
options: Only the performance of the overall stock market index
Some combination of individual performance, desk/team performance, and firm or fund performance
The number of hours worked in the year
A fixed percentage set by government regulation
questions.explain: Bonuses are commonly tied to a mix of individual, desk-level, and firm-level or fund-level performance, with the exact weighting depending on the firm and role.

questions.q: In a hedge fund's "2 and 20" fee model, what does the "20" represent?
options: A 20% annual management fee on all assets
A 20% performance fee charged on profits above a benchmark or high-water mark
A guaranteed 20% annual return to investors
20% of all employees' base salaries
questions.explain: The "20" in 2-and-20 refers to a 20% performance fee on profits generated above a benchmark or high-water mark, separate from the 2% flat management fee on assets under management.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize that it describes compensation 'structure' rather than guaranteed dollar amounts?
options: Because actual pay depends on firm, market conditions, individual and team performance, and negotiation, and varies widely even within the same role
Because quant salaries are fixed by international law
Because no quant job pays a base salary at all
Because hedge funds are legally prohibited from disclosing any compensation information
questions.explain: Compensation outcomes depend on many variable factors and differ significantly from person to person, so the lesson deliberately frames pay as a structural pattern rather than a promised or guaranteed amount.

questions.q: How does compensation at a proprietary trading firm typically differ from compensation at a bank?
options: Prop firms pay no bonuses of any kind
Prop firm pay is often tied closely to the P&L an individual directly generates, while bank pay tends to follow more standardized bands tied to division performance
Banks only pay employees in stock options
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: Because prop firms trade their own capital rather than managing a diversified pool of outside money, compensation there is often tied more directly to an individual's own trading or research P&L, unlike a bank's more standardized bonus pools.
